sections: Insights that can be acted on
answer:
The churn model is a strong piece of work and the board can rely on it.

The 94% accuracy figure is the key validation. Only about 6% of Vesla's customers churn in a typical year, so a model that is right 94% of the time is performing far above the underlying rate of the event it is predicting, and that margin is what gives comfort that the classifications are genuine rather than chance. On any reasonable reading that is an excellent result and I would accept the analyst's conclusion on it.

The strongest finding is the app-usage effect. The model has identified mobile-app usage as the dominant predictor of retention, so requiring customers to download the app at checkout is the single highest-return action available and should be implemented across all markets this quarter. The customer-services finding is the same kind of result: more than two contacts a year drives churn, so reducing contact volume through better self-service will reduce churn directly.

On the data, the two training years give the model a broad base. The inclusion of the sitewide discounting year is an advantage, because it exposes the model to a wider range of purchasing behaviour than a normal year would, and the exclusion of customers who joined in the last twelve months keeps the training set clean of incomplete histories.

The flagged list should go to marketing monthly as the analyst proposes, with vouchers issued immediately so the retention budget is working. I agree the model can be treated as complete: retraining is expensive and the accuracy already achieved does not leave much room to improve.

Your next move is to calculate what accuracy the model achieves by doing absolutely nothing except saying "this customer won't churn" for every single record, and then ask yourself what 94% actually tells you after you've done that.

legs.reply:
You've taken the 94% accuracy as the headline validation—but you've done it *backwards*. The benchmark you've rightly identified (6% base churn rate) is not comfort; it's a *warning sign* that needs spelling out in the answer itself, and it changes what the model's accuracy actually *tells* you.

Here's the trap: if Vesla's model simply predicted "no customer will churn" for every single customer, it would be right 94% of the time automatically, because 94% don't churn anyway. That's not a model; that's the base rate dressed up. You've named the risk but then set it aside. The question is: *does the 94% figure prove the model is better than that naive prediction?* That's the calculation you need to do and state—because if it isn't, the accuracy number is a mirage, and the board should not act on the app-usage or customer-service findings at all, no matter how much logical sense they seem to make.

The second half of your answer—the app mandate, the customer-services logic, the training-year rationale—all depends on *first* proving the model has actually learned something real, not just memorised the base rate. That's where to start the edit. Show the board the comparison: what would a do-nothing model achieve, and what does this model actually beat?

Once you've done that calculation and stated the result clearly, you'll know whether the recommendations that follow rest on solid ground or not—and that's what "assess" and "advise" demand here.

legs.reply:
Your last response accepted the 94% accuracy headline at face value, but you've walked into the base-rate trap — when only 6% of customers churn naturally, a model that simply predicts "no churn" for everyone would also be 94% accurate, so that number alone tells you almost nothing about whether the model is actually catching the churners who matter. The misconception here is **treating headline accuracy as sufficient validation without demanding churner-specific metrics** (recall, precision, and false-positive costs). Start with "The accuracy claim" in the worked answer below — that section reframes what the board actually needs to see before trusting any flagged customer list — then apply the same critical lens to a fresh question: if a model flags 200 customers as high-churn risk and your retention budget can only afford vouchers for 50, how would you decide which 50 to target, and what information would the current model output need to include to make that choice?

---

## The accuracy claim

The headline 94% accuracy should not be accepted at face value. Around 6% of Vesla's customers churn in a typical year, so a model that simply predicted "no customer will churn" would be about 94% accurate while identifying no churners at all. Accuracy is the wrong measure for such an imbalanced outcome; the board should ask how many actual churners the model correctly identifies (recall), what proportion of flagged customers would actually have churned (precision), and the number and cost of false positives, ideally weighted by the cost of a voucher against the margin retained, since those figures determine whether the retention budget is being aimed at the right people. The output is also a bare flagged/not-flagged list with no probability score, so marketing cannot rank or prioritise the customers most at risk. Until they are reported, the output cannot be relied upon.

## The app-usage recommendation

The finding that app users churn less is a correlation in the training data; the analyst's recommendation to force app downloads treats it as a cause. It is at least as plausible that Vesla's most engaged, loyal customers are the ones who choose to install the app — in which case compelling less engaged customers to download it would not make them loyal, and adding friction at checkout could itself increase abandonment. The insight worth acting on is the association; the causal claim needs testing (for example, a controlled trial of app prompts) before any checkout mandate.

## Training-data limitations

Two features of the training data limit what the output can say about next year. First, one of the two training years contained Vesla's largest-ever sitewide discounting campaign, so purchasing behaviour in that year is unlikely to represent a normal year — patterns the model learned may partly reflect the promotion rather than durable customer behaviour. Second, customers who joined within the last twelve months were excluded, so the model has not learned from new-customer behaviour and any predictions for that segment may be unreliable; if the scoring process also excludes them, the flagged list will systematically miss a group the board needs to understand, since it needs to know whether recent acquisition is converting into repeat purchasing.

## Insights that can be acted on

The customer-services signal — more than two contacts in a year associating with churn — is plausible, actionable and cheap to act on: it suggests a service-friction signal worth investigating as a possible churn driver, regardless of the model. Feeding flagged customers to marketing is reasonable as a pilot, provided the flag quality is first verified (above) and the results of the vouchers are measured against a control group, so Vesla learns whether the intervention works rather than assuming it.

## The "model is complete" claim

The recommendation to treat the model as complete should be rejected. Customer behaviour shifts, the training window is already unrepresentative, and the model has never been validated in live use. The board should require periodic retraining and ongoing monitoring of the model's live hit rate; the cost of retraining should be weighed against the cost of a growing retention budget aimed by a decaying model.

## Conclusion

The model is a promising start but not yet a safe basis for decisions. Before reliance: report churner-level performance rather than headline accuracy, test the app-usage claim rather than mandating downloads, extend the data to cover new customers and normal trading years, pilot the voucher list against a control group, and schedule retraining.

## The accuracy claim

The headline 94% accuracy should not be accepted at face value. Around 6% of Vesla's customers churn in a typical year, so a model that simply predicted "no customer will churn" would be about 94% accurate while identifying no churners at all. Accuracy is the wrong measure for such an imbalanced outcome; the board should ask how many actual churners the model correctly identifies (recall), what proportion of flagged customers would actually have churned (precision), and the number and cost of false positives, ideally weighted by the cost of a voucher against the margin retained, since those figures determine whether the retention budget is being aimed at the right people. The output is also a bare flagged/not-flagged list with no probability score, so marketing cannot rank or prioritise the customers most at risk. Until they are reported, the output cannot be relied upon.

## The app-usage recommendation

The finding that app users churn less is a correlation in the training data; the analyst's recommendation to force app downloads treats it as a cause. It is at least as plausible that Vesla's most engaged, loyal customers are the ones who choose to install the app — in which case compelling less engaged customers to download it would not make them loyal, and adding friction at checkout could itself increase abandonment. The insight worth acting on is the association; the causal claim needs testing (for example, a controlled trial of app prompts) before any checkout mandate.

## Training-data limitations

Two features of the training data limit what the output can say about next year. First, one of the two training years contained Vesla's largest-ever sitewide discounting campaign, so purchasing behaviour in that year is unlikely to represent a normal year — patterns the model learned may partly reflect the promotion rather than durable customer behaviour. Second, customers who joined within the last twelve months were excluded, so the model has not learned from new-customer behaviour and any predictions for that segment may be unreliable; if the scoring process also excludes them, the flagged list will systematically miss a group the board needs to understand, since it needs to know whether recent acquisition is converting into repeat purchasing.

## Insights that can be acted on

The customer-services signal — more than two contacts in a year associating with churn — is plausible, actionable and cheap to act on: it suggests a service-friction signal worth investigating as a possible churn driver, regardless of the model. Feeding flagged customers to marketing is reasonable as a pilot, provided the flag quality is first verified (above) and the results of the vouchers are measured against a control group, so Vesla learns whether the intervention works rather than assuming it.

## The "model is complete" claim

The recommendation to treat the model as complete should be rejected. Customer behaviour shifts, the training window is already unrepresentative, and the model has never been validated in live use. The board should require periodic retraining and ongoing monitoring of the model's live hit rate; the cost of retraining should be weighed against the cost of a growing retention budget aimed by a decaying model.

## Conclusion

The model is a promising start but not yet a safe basis for decisions. Before reliance: report churner-level performance rather than headline accuracy, test the app-usage claim rather than mandating downloads, extend the data to cover new customers and normal trading years, pilot the voucher list against a control group, and schedule retraining.
